hypotheses: Globalization contributes to deindustrialization through both direct and indirect effects.
Rising consumer affluence leads to increased demand for services rather than manufactured goods, contributing to deindustrialization.
claim.statement: This study analyzes why the world’s most economically advanced countries have deindustrialized over the last few decades.

data.source: OECD STAN Database, International Trade by Commodities Database, United Nations National Accounts Main Aggregates Database
data.notes: The study analyzes panel data from multiple databases; measures include real income per capita, productivity growth differential, trade as a percentage of GDP.

method.description: The analysis uses panel data from 18 OECD countries spanning a period from 1970 to 2003 to test three explanations for deindustrialization using fixed-effects regression models.
steps: Collect panel data for 18 OECD countries from 1970 to 2003.
Identify and define dependent and independent variables, including national affluence, unbalanced productivity growth, and trade statistics.
Estimate direct and indirect effects on relative manufacturing employment using fixed-effects generalized least squares (FE-GLS) regression.
Incorporate controls for fixed effects, period effects, and unemployment.
Interpret results to determine the relative importance of each factor on deindustrialization.
method.independent_variables: National affluence, unbalanced productivity growth, imports and exports from North-South trade
method.tools_software: Stata, using xtgls command for GLS estimation

results.summary: Each of the three factors—rising affluence, productivity growth differentials, and globalization—significantly contribute to deindustrialization. Global trade exerts both direct and indirect effects, but rising consumer affluence is the greatest factor.

metadata.original_paper_title: Explaining Deindustrialization: How Affluence, Productivity Growth, and Globalization Diminish Manufacturing Employment
